Hi Ken,

I'm retackling this issue and wonder if you could help with a few quick questions. I've run detection probability on some of the seasons that didn't work and while they are low (as low as 0.031), they do not differ much from seasons that do work (as low as 0.037).

Does Unmarked have a threshold for how low detection probability can be to run?

Right now my J value is high, 90 to 92, because I am using 24 hour periods and analyzing my results by seasons. Do you think it would be helpful to bin the time interval into weeks so that J would be around 12? Or would that not be a good idea because I am looking at species interactions?

Thank you so much for any insight you may have.

Rachel

messages.body_plain:
Rachel,

There's no specific threshold, but the lower the p the more likely you are to run into issues. I would expect that even if your model successfully converges with p~0.05, your parameter estimates may have gigantic standard errors and thus won't be particularly useful. Looking back at your previous email, did you identify specific covariates that seemed to be contributing to your problems?

I think it's probably worth trying a weekly time interval. It shouldn't greatly change inference about occupancy at the site (which is over the entire period, regardless of how you break it up into smaller pieces). Regardless, you have to be careful when thinking about what any "interactions" mean - eg even if two species seem to occupy the same sites based on your analysis, you can't necessarily say they are *directly* interacting with each other. They might be active at completely different times, etc. This model can't address those kinds of questions.

Ken

messages.subject: Parboot function
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I did the goodness of fit test for my global model :
>mod_global <- occu(~PV_5m + Sentier_cerf ~ Enclo + Strate +  pr_Cornus_c_center + s_terriere_gaule_EB_center, data=UFO1)
>UFO1 <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=dect, siteCovs= cov[,-3])

The code using parboot function is:
>set.seed(1234)
>chisq <- function(fm) {
  observed <- getY(fm@data)
  expected <- fitted(fm)
  sum((observed - expected)^2/expected, na.rm = TRUE)
}
>pb <- parboot(mod_global, statistic = chisq, nsim = 1000)
>pb

The results are:
Call: parboot(object = mod_global, statistic = chisq, nsim = 1000)

Parametric Bootstrap Statistics:
    t0 mean(t0 - t_B) StdDev(t0 - t_B) Pr(t_B > t0)
1 1433          -12.6             53.3        0.594

t_B quantiles:
       0% 2.5%  25%  50%  75% 97.5% 100%
[1,] 1265 1355 1417 1442 1469  1552 1964

t0 = Original statistic computed from data
t_B = Vector of bootstrap samples

My question is: How do I interpret these results, is global model presenting a lack of fit? What does t0= 1433 mean? What is Pr(t B > t0)= 0.594 mean?

Thank you,
Aimie

messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Parboot function
messages.body_plain:
Aimie,

If you're using occupancy models, you can't compute a Pearson chi-square on the data (see McCullagh and Nelder 1989). You need to aggregate the data into groups. For example, the MacKenzie and Bailey goodness of fit test aggregates data over the different detection histories and compares observed and expected frequencies of each.

Best,

Marc

messages.subject_clean: Goodness of fit error for hierarchical distance modeling
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm consistently getting the same error when running a GOF test for my top ranked hierarchical distance model for a songbird species. The error is "Error in checkForRemoteErrors(val) : 4 nodes produced errors; first error: non-finite finite-difference value [7]". Weirdly, when I ran this seem code weeks ago it worked perfectly fine and I ran this same code for eight other species and it worked. The model looks like this:

lambda.global1 <- gdistsamp(~horzveg+rubus+vertveg+fern, ~1, ~observer, keyfun = "halfnorm", output = "density", unitsOut = "ha", mixture = "P", K = 100, se = TRUE, data = umf1)

The code for the GOF test:

fitstats <- function(fm) {
    observed <- getY(fm@data)
    expected <- fitted(fm)
    resids <- residuals(fm)
    sse <- sum(resids^2)
    chisq <- sum((observed - expected)^2 / expected)
    freeTuke <- sum((sqrt(observed) - sqrt(expected))^2)
    out <- c(SSE=sse, Chisq=chisq, freemanTukey=freeTuke)
    return(out)
}
(gof.final <- parboot(lambda.global1, fitstats, nsim=100, report=5))
(c.hat <- gof.final@t0[2]/mean(gof....@t.star[,2]))

Has anyone else run into this issue? I've tried running the GOF test using different models with only one parameter and it still does not work. Thanks in advance.

messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Spatial autocorrelation amongst the camera sites
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Spatial autocorrelation amongst the camera sites
messages.body_plain:
Dear Aye,

you can't accommodate spatial autocorrelation in unmarked, but you could try the R packages hSDM or stocc which do offer that. For the latter, see the paper by Johnson et al. in Ecology in 2013. Alternatively, as always, you could use JAGS, Nimble or Stan. Our new AHM2 book has a chapter on spatial autocorrelation in occupancy and Nmix models and shows the fitting of CAR models and models with splines in JAGS and WinBUGS.

Ken Kellner has the UBMS package in the pipeline which does models like unmarked, but allows additional random effects. I don't believe that UBSM currently allows for models with spatial dependence, but I may be wrong.

You could perhaps also choose to ignore the non-independence induced by the same animal being detectable by more than one trap. The typical rule of thumb about many types of non-independence is that ignoring it will usually bias low the SEs of your estimates, but not necessarily the point estimate. Depending on the goals of your modeling, this may be acceptable ?

But why not give stocc a try ?

I don't know what to think about this: "... stations ... are not representatively laid across the study area." This hasn't gotten anything to do with spatial autocorrelation and could be a bigger pain for the interpretation of your results. You can estimate some parameters, but you may not be able to define any general area to which these estimates refer to other than the specific trapping area. But perhaps that is good enough.

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Dear Marc,
I really thank you so much for your great answer. I have read the  paper by Johnson et al. in Ecology in 2013 and also trying to use "stocc". However, I am not familiar with  Bayesian theory and also the use of "WinBUGS". I am  reading your book " Introduction to WinBUGS for Ecologists". It is very helpful and useful especially for me who do not have any background knowledge about Bayesian theory and WinBUGS. I still cannot reach to AHM book.
Regarding this matter, may I kindly know whether you have any plan to conduct a workshop/training/lecture (via online) about  WinBUGS .
Again, I really thank you for giving a warm help  whenever we have any analytical problems in unmarked.
Best Regards,
Aye

On Monday, December 14, 2020 at 4:20:45 PM UTC+8 Kery Marc wrote:
> Dear Aye,
>
> you can't accommodate spatial autocorrelation in unmarked, but you could try the R packages hSDM or stocc which do offer that. For the latter, see the paper by Johnson et al. in Ecology in 2013. Alternatively, as always, you could use JAGS, Nimble or Stan. Our new AHM2 book has a chapter on spatial autocorrelation in occupancy and Nmix models and shows the fitting of CAR models and models with splines in JAGS and WinBUGS.
>
> Ken Kellner has the UBMS package in the pipeline which does models like unmarked, but allows additional random effects. I don't believe that UBSM currently allows for models with spatial dependence, but I may be wrong.
>
> You could perhaps also choose to ignore the non-independence induced by the same animal being detectable by more than one trap. The typical rule of thumb about many types of non-independence is that ignoring it will usually bias low the SEs of your estimates, but not necessarily the point estimate. Depending on the goals of your modeling, this may be acceptable ?
>
> But why not give stocc a try ?
>
> I don't know what to think about this: "... stations ... are not representatively laid across the study area." This hasn't gotten anything to do with spatial autocorrelation and could be a bigger pain for the interpretation of your results. You can estimate some parameters, but you may not be able to define any general area to which these estimates refer to other than the specific trapping area. But perhaps that is good enough.
>
> Best regards  -- Marc
>
>
>

Hi Ken,

My human rates covariate was the problem. I ran the model without covariates, it worked, and then added them back in and was able to determine just one species that was causing the error.

I'm working on converting a season to the weekly time interval now. Thanks for the tips on interactions, I am definitely keeping that in mind.

Rachel

El mié, 2 de dic. de 2020 a la(s) 11:09, Ken Kellner (ken.k...@gmail.com) escribió:

> Rachel,
>
> There's no specific threshold, but the lower the p the more likely you are to run into issues. I would expect that even if your model successfully converges with p~0.05, your parameter estimates may have gigantic standard errors and thus won't be particularly useful. Looking back at your previous email, did you identify specific covariates that seemed to be contributing to your problems?
>
> I think it's probably worth trying a weekly time interval. It shouldn't greatly change inference about occupancy at the site (which is over the entire period, regardless of how you break it up into smaller pieces). Regardless, you have to be careful when thinking about what any "interactions" mean - eg even if two species seem to occupy the same sites based on your analysis, you can't necessarily say they are *directly* interacting with each other. They might be active at completely different times, etc. This model can't address those kinds of questions.
>
> Ken
>

> > Hi Ken,
> >

> >
> > Does Unmarked have a threshold for how low detection probability can be to run?
> >
> > Right now my J value is high, 90 to 92, because I am using 24 hour periods and analyzing my results by seasons. Do you think it would be helpful to bin the time interval into weeks so that J would be around 12? Or would that not be a good idea because I am looking at species interactions?
> >
> > Thank you so much for any insight you may have.
> >
> > Rachel
> >
> > On Saturday, May 30, 2020 at 3:15:33 PM UTC-7 Rachel Townsend wrote:
> > > Hi Ken,
> > >
> > > I posted a summary table of my data above - I'm not sure why Spring 2017 and Summer season was cut off so I attached it as a word file. I thought it might be the lack of number of detections that was causing the problem as well; however, it is strange that for example, that Winter 2016 worked while winter 2015 did not. I'm a bit stumped. I did try fitting the model without covariates (human detection rate and on trail/off trail) and it did work so I guess now I should try adding in one covariate at a time to see when it generates the error. messages.subject: Job advertisement: pattern recognition in acoustic monitoring in Sempach/Switzerland
messages.subject_clean: Job advertisement: pattern recognition in acoustic monitoring in Sempach/Switzerland
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

here is a potentially interesting job advertisement. At the Swiss ornithological institute at Sempach/Switzerland, we are looking for a person to develop and organize an acoustic monitoring program for birds. A significant part of the work will be number crunching to explore and further develop the algorithms for automatic pattern recognition, presumably followed by some occupancy modeling or similar. The downside, for a large part of the audience in these two lists, is that you must be really fluent in either German or French and also have some knowledge of the other of these two languages.

https://www.vogelwarte.ch/de/vogelwarte/mitarbeit/jobs/wissenschaftliche-mitarbeiterin-/-wissenschaftlicher-mitarbeiter-akustisches-monitoring

Please consider to apply if you qualify and are interested.

Best regards  -- Marc

_____________________________________________________________

Marc Kéry
+41 41 462 97 93
marc...@vogelwarte.ch
www.vogelwarte.ch <http://www.vogelwarte.ch>
Swiss Ornithological Institute | Seerose 1 | CH-6204 Sempach | Switzerland
